title: Library Index Audit
story: A library's search kiosk finds books with a binary search tree of shelf numbers: at each node it goes left for smaller numbers and right for larger ones, skipping a whole branch each step. That only works if the tree is laid out correctly.
Volunteers edited the tree by hand over the summer. Before the kiosk goes back online, audit it: is every shelf number still where the kiosk will find it?
task: Write indexIsValid(root). Return true if the tree is a valid binary search tree, else false. Valid means: for every node, every value in its left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's value, and every value in its right subtree is strictly larger. Equal values anywhere make it invalid.
An empty tree is valid. Trees are shown in level order, like [50, 30, 70, 20, 40], with null for a missing child. Your function receives real TreeNode objects with val, left and right.
constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep.

examples.explanation: Everything under 30 (20, 40) is below 50, everything under 70 (60, 80) is above 50, and each small family is in order. A search for 60 goes right at 50, left at 70, and finds it.
55 is the right child of 30, and 55 > 30, so that pair looks fine. But 55 is in 50's left subtree, where every number must be below 50. A search for 55 would go right at 50 and never find it.

hints: In the second example, every parent and child pair looks correct on its own. Which ancestor does 55 disagree with?
Checking against the parent is not enough. Each node has a range of allowed values set by all its ancestors. What is the range where 55 sits?
Stepping left from a node with value v makes v the upper limit. Stepping right makes v the lower limit. The other limit is inherited.

Recurse with (node, low, high), starting with no limits. A null node is valid. A node is invalid if val <= low or val >= high. Otherwise check the left child with (low, val) and the right with (val, high). Use null (or infinity) for "no limit", not the smallest or largest shelf number, because those can appear in the tree.
bruteForce: For each node, scan its whole left subtree to confirm everything is smaller, and its right subtree to confirm everything is larger.

A node near the top scans almost the whole tree; a chain of 1,000 nodes costs about 500,000 comparisons, O(n²). Deep nodes get rechecked against every ancestor separately. Carrying the tightest limits down checks each node once.

* TreeNode is already defined for you.
* @return {boolean} true if the tree is a valid binary search tree

tests.note: defeats parent-only check (6 under 15 but right of 10)
deep grandchild breaks the root's limit
defeats using the min/max value as 'no limit'

js: // low and high are exclusive limits; null means no limit.
if (low !== null && node.val <= low) return false;
if (high !== null && node.val >= high) return false;
return check(node.left, low, node.val)    // left: new upper limit
&& check(node.right, node.val, high);   // right: new lower limit

walkthrough: Every node lives inside a window of allowed values. The root's window is open on both sides. Going left caps the window at the parent's value; going right sets its floor.
1. 50: window (none, none). Fine. Left child gets (none, 50), right child (50, none).
• 30: window (none, 50). Fine. Left child gets (none, 30), right child (30, 50).
The window at 55 remembers both its parent (30) and grandparent (50), exactly what a parent-only check throws away.
solution.timeWhy: Each node is checked once against two numbers.
solution.spaceWhy: The recursion stack, one call per level; h is the tree's height.
solution.takeaway: When a rule involves all ancestors, not just the parent, pass a summary of them down as parameters (here a low and high limit). For search trees, an in-order walk checking that values strictly increase works equally well.
